readerTitle: Ben & Jerry's sold the company but tried to keep its soul
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Ben & Jerry's, Unilever, 2000년 매각과 이후 갈등) + 가상 적용 (대기업에 인수되는 소프트웨어 팀)
insight: 매각 계약에 적은 약속은 보호 장치일 뿐 통제권이 아니다. 팔고 나서 무엇이 지켜질지는 조건의 구체성, 기한, 그리고 최종 결정권을 누가 갖는지가 정한다.
misconception: 좋은 조건을 계약에 넣으면 매각 후에도 창업자의 가치와 독립성이 영원히 지켜진다. 또는 창업자가 원하지 않으면 회사는 팔리지 않는다.

sources.text: Unilever press release, 12 April 2000: agreement to acquire Ben & Jerry's Homemade (about $326 million, $43.60 per share)
The New York Times, April 2000 coverage of the Unilever deal and the founders' reluctance
Ben & Jerry's company history (founded 1978 in Burlington, Vermont; three-part mission)
Reuters and other major news coverage, 2021–2022: West Bank sales decision and Unilever's sale of the Israeli business to its local licensee
Reuters and other major news coverage, 2025: Magnum Ice Cream Company spin-off, CEO removal, Jerry Greenfield's resignation letter

factChecks.note: 인수가 약 3억 2,600만 달러, 주당 43.60달러(2000년 4월 발표)는 Unilever 보도자료로 재확인하세요. 카드에는 "about $326 million"으로 적었습니다.
Ben Cohen이 투자자들과 대항 인수안을 꾸리려 했다는 점, 이사회가 주주 소송 위험을 의식했다는 점은 당시 보도에 널리 나오지만 세부(참여 투자자, 제시 가격)는 카드에 쓰지 않았습니다. 다른 입찰자(예: Dreyer's) 언급도 생략했습니다.
인수 조건: 브랜드의 사회적 사명과 무결성을 책임지는 독립 이사회 유지, 재단 기부와 버몬트 기반 관련 약속. 정확한 기부 금액·기간은 확인되지 않아 카드에 수치 없이 서술했습니다.
창업자들의 지분이 이사회 결정을 단독으로 막을 수준이 아니었다는 서술은 정성적 표현입니다. 정확한 지분율은 쓰지 않았습니다.
2021년 서안 지구 판매 중단 발표, 2022년 Unilever의 이스라엘 사업 현지 라이선시 매각, 이후 소송, 2025년 아이스크림 사업 분사와 CEO 교체, 2025년 9월 Jerry Greenfield 사임은 게시 직전 최신 보도로 다시 확인하세요. 진행 중인 사안이라 카드에 평가를 넣지 않았습니다.
이사회의 법적 의무는 국가·주별로 다르므로 일반적인 원리로만 설명했고 법률 조언으로 읽히지 않게 했습니다.

cards.title: Ben & Jerry's sold the company but tried to keep its soul
body: Ben & Jerry's began in 1978 in a converted gas station in Burlington, Vermont. It grew into a brand famous for chunky flavors and loud social causes.
In 2000, it agreed to be bought by Unilever, one of the world's largest consumer goods companies. The founders reportedly didn't want to sell. The deal happened anyway.

image.label: A small ice cream shop in an old gas station facing a giant factory
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 왼쪽에 개조한 작은 주유소 아이스크림 가게, 오른쪽에 거대한 공장 건물. 둘 사이에 계약서 한 장이 떠 있음. 실제 로고, 브랜드 포장, 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: A big buyer offers far more than your share price.
body: It's 2000. You co-founded the company, and it trades on the stock market. Big food companies want to buy it at a price well above what the shares are worth today.
You want to stay independent. But your shares alone can't decide what the board does. What do you push for?

options.text: Refuse every offer and tell the board to stay independent
options.feedback: It keeps your hands clean, but the board answers to all shareholders, not just you. Turning down a large premium can invite lawsuits, and you may end up with no say in the terms.

options.text: Accept that a sale may come, and fight for written protections in the deal
options.feedback: You trade full independence for a voice in the terms. You keep some of what matters, but only what you manage to get on paper.

options.text: Find friendly investors to make a rival offer
options.feedback: A friendlier owner could protect the mission. But the rival bid has to compete on price, and that's hard to win against a giant.

cards.title: The board said yes. The founders shaped the terms.
body: Ben Cohen reportedly tried to put together an investor group to buy the company himself. It didn't come together in time. In April 2000, the board accepted Unilever's offer of **about $326 million**.

The deal had unusual terms for its time. Ben & Jerry's kept an independent board responsible for its social mission and brand integrity. Unilever also made commitments on the company's charitable foundation and its base in Vermont.

cards.title: Selling shares means sharing the exit decision.
body: When you take outside owners, especially public shareholders, **the decision to sell is no longer only yours**. The board's job is to weigh offers for all owners. A big premium is hard to refuse.
So the founders' real choice in 2000 wasn't "sell or don't." It was "what can we protect if we're sold?" That question started years earlier, when they first sold shares to outsiders.

image.label: A founder holding one key among many keys held by others
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 큰 자물쇠 하나에 열쇠 구멍이 여러 개. 창업자 캐릭터가 열쇠 하나를 들고 있고, 나머지 열쇠는 "Shareholders", "Board" 라벨의 손들이 들고 있음. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: For years, the protections mostly held.
body: The independent board gave the brand a formal voice inside a huge company. Ben & Jerry's kept speaking out on social issues and kept its own style for a long time after the sale.
This is the middle path most acquired founders get. Not control, but **written rights**: who decides what, and what the new owner promised not to do.

cards.title: A promise isn't the same as power.
body: In 2021, Ben & Jerry's said it would stop selling in Israeli-occupied West Bank areas. In 2022, Unilever sold the Israeli business to its local licensee. Ben & Jerry's board sued.
In 2025, as Unilever spun off its ice cream business, the brand's CEO was removed. Co-founder Jerry Greenfield resigned, saying the brand's independence was gone.
Written terms can protect a mission. When the parties disagree hard, the owner usually has the final word.

image.label: A contract stretched between two hands, starting to tear
image.brief: 계약서 한 장을 작은 손과 큰 손이 양쪽에서 잡아당기고, 가운데가 살짝 찢어지기 시작함. 차분한 색감, 실제 로고나 브랜드 없음.

cards.title: Now your software team is joining a bigger company.
body: You run a 12-person team behind a well-loved scheduling app. A large company wants to buy it and make your team a unit inside. They say, "You'll keep running your own roadmap."
What do you secure before signing?

options.text: Nothing extra. Their promise and your culture will carry it
options.feedback: Friendly words cost the buyer nothing. When leaders or priorities change, there's nothing to point to.

options.text: Written budget, decision rights and how long they last, plus a clear plan for when they end
options.feedback: You get real protection for a known period, and you stop expecting the deal to give you control forever.

options.text: Keep the app's name and brand unchanged
options.feedback: The brand survives, but a name protects how things look, not who decides what gets built.

cards.title: After a sale, you keep only what's written down, and only until the owner disagrees.
body: Ben & Jerry's shows the best a reluctant seller usually gets: strong terms, not lasting control. Decide what you must protect before you take outside owners.
**Try it today:** write the three things you'd most want to stay true if your business or team had a new owner. Next to each, note who could overrule it.
